The Tariff Revisions also include provisions relevant to the resource adequacy concerns that

14, 2026.  As explained in Section VII of this transmittal letter, this effective date will allow all 
affected parties to prepare to take advantage of the new transmission services for Large Loads.

submitted as part of this filing (both described in Section IV.B.3 of this filing letter) are supported by 
the Testimony of Dennis Cakert.  All other Tariff Revisions submitted as part of this filing under the 
ISO’s section 205 rights are supported by the Affidavit of Alexander Rost (both are solely sponsored 
by the ISO).   
 
I. 
DESCRIPTION OF THE FILING PARTIES AND COMMUNICATIONS 
ISO-NE is the private, non-profit entity that serves as the Regional Transmission 
Organization (“RTO”) for New England.  ISO-NE plans and operates the New England bulk power 
system and administers New England’s organized wholesale electricity markets pursuant to the 
Tariff and the Transmission Operating Agreement (“TOA”) with the PTOs.  In its capacity as an 
RTO, ISO-NE has the responsibility to protect the short-term reliability of the New England

NEPOOL is a voluntary association organized in 1971 pursuant to the NEPOOL 
Agreement, and it has grown to include more than 560 members.  The Participants include all of 
the electric utilities rendering or receiving service under the ISO-NE Tariff, as well as independent 
power generators, marketers, load aggregators, brokers, consumer-owned utility systems, end 
users, developers, demand resource providers, and a merchant transmission provider.  Pursuant to 
revised governance provisions accepted by the Commission,8 the Participants act through the 
NEPOOL Participants Committee.  The Participants Committee is authorized by Section 6.1 of 
the Second Restated NEPOOL Agreement and Section 8.1.3(c) of the Participants Agreement to 
represent NEPOOL in proceedings before the Commission.  Pursuant to Section 2.2 of the 
Participants Agreement, “NEPOOL provide[s] the sole Participant Processes for advisory voting 
on [ISO-NE] matters and the selection of [ISO-NE] Board members, except for input from state 
regulatory authorities and as otherwise may be provided in the [ISO-NE] Tariff, TOA and the 
Market Participant Services Agreement included in the [ISO-NE] Tariff.” 
The PTOs9 are Transmission Providers providing Local Service on an open-access basis 
under Schedule 21 of the OATT. Pursuant to the terms of the TOA among the PTOs and ISO-NE, 
the PTOs own, physically operate and maintain Transmission Facilities in New England and ISO-
NE has Operating Authority (as defined in Section 3.02 of the TOA) over all of the Transmission 
Facilities of the PTOs, including those used to provide Local Service under Schedule 21 of the 
OATT.  Section 3.04 of the TOA also grants the PTOs authority to submit filings to the 
Commission pursuant to section 205 of the FPA in matters affecting the rates, terms and conditions 
of Local Service under Schedule 21 and rates and charges, including cost allocation, for Regional 
Transmission Service under the OATT. 
Schedule 21 of the ISO OATT comprises two distinct parts.  First, under the common 
provisions of Schedule 21 (“Schedule 21–Common”), the PTOs have collectively accumulated the 
common terms and conditions of Local Service applicable to transmission service over the local 
facilities of all of the PTOs.  Second, each PTO has its own individual Schedule 21 schedule 
(“Local Service Schedule”), containing the rates, terms and conditions applicable to service over 
the Local Facilities owned by that particular PTO. The Schedule 21 Local Service Schedules

II. 
STANDARD OF REVIEW 
The Tariff Revisions are submitted pursuant to section 205 of the FPA, which “gives a utility 
the right to file rates and terms for services rendered with its assets.”11  Under section 205, the 
Commission “plays ‘an essentially passive and reactive’ role”’12 whereby it “can reject [a filing] only 
if it finds that the changes proposed by the public utility are not ‘just and reasonable.’”13  The 
Commission limits this inquiry “into whether the rates proposed by a utility are reasonable – and [this 
inquiry does not] extend to determining whether a proposed rate schedule is more or less reasonable 
than alternative rate designs.”14  The revisions filed herein “need not be the only reasonable

III. 
BACKGROUND AND EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
A. 
Background 
The Show Cause Order is one of six show cause orders that the Commission simultaneously 
issued to all six RTO and Independent System Operators to address large and co-located load issues.  In

show cause as to why the Tariff remains just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or 
preferential without provisions addressing:   
(a) 
the application process, study procedures, and ongoing operational requirements that 
apply to Eligible Customers seeking transmission service on behalf of large loads;17  
(b) 
additional transparency concerning the network upgrade costs to provide transmission 
service to Eligible Customers on behalf of large loads, a pro forma cost recovery 
agreement between ISO-NE, the relevant transmission owner and Eligible Customer 
taking transmission service on behalf of the large load to mitigate the risk of cost shifting 
among transmission customers, and a mechanism to ensure such payments are 
appropriately credited towards transmission owners’ transmission revenue 
requirements consistent with the Commission’s cost-of-service regulations;  
(c) 
the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to co-location arrangements;  
(d)

B. 
Executive Summary 
1. 
The Tariff Revisions Address the Five Categories of Reform in the Show 
Cause Order 
The Filing Parties submit that the Tariff Revisions address all of the Commission’s concerns in 
each of the five categories of reform of the Show Cause Order (i.e., efficient study processes, co-location 
rules, flexible load service, generation studies, and cost transparency).     
   
a. Efficient Study Processes 
To address this category of reform, the Tariff Revisions include a definition of Large Load, 
which is based on the characteristics of ISO-NE’s transmission system.  The definition includes a 50 
MW load size, and a 60 kV interconnection voltage threshold.27  The ISO also developed exclusions 
from the definition based on the characteristics of the load, exclusions in other regions, and stakeholder 
feedback.  Importantly, as described in Section IV.B.1 of this transmittal letter, the Tariff Revisions 
include language that accommodates the transition of a load into the definition of Large Load and 
accommodates existing commercial arrangements. 
 
In addition, the Tariff Revisions include an application process that applies to Large Load 
Eligible Customers seeking transmission service on behalf of Large Loads.  This process requires a non-
refundable application fee and sufficient readiness requirements to deter duplicative or speculative

Moreover, the Tariff Revisions include operational requirements for Large Load Transmission 
Customers seeking transmission service on behalf of Large Loads, including the provision of hourly 
forecasts, telemetry data, communication channels, installation of equipment to enable the ISO to 
monitor the impacts of Large Loads, ramp-rate and ride-through requirements, and requirements for 
protection systems to limit withdrawals from the transmission system.  Under the operational 
requirements, ISO-NE will also be able to coordinate the remote disconnection of a Large Load to 
maintain reliability of the transmission system.   
 
Finally, the Tariff Revisions include a pro forma Large Load Transmission Service Agreement, 
as well as a pro forma Large Load System Impact Study Agreement and a pro forma Large Load 
Facilities Study Agreement.   
 
b. Co-location Rules 
To address this category of reform, the ISO is proposing a definition of Behind-the-Meter 
Generation along with a netting threshold of zero MW for Large Loads.  Effectively, the Tariff 
Revisions prohibit the netting of a Large Load with Behind-the-Meter Generation for settlement of 
wholesale services.  In addition, as explained in the next category of reform below, the ISO has 
developed transmission services that recognize the ability of Large Loads (including co-located loads) 
to limit withdrawal from the transmission system under certain conditions. 
 
c. Flexible Load Service 
The Tariff Revisions include three new transmission services: firm transmission service for 
Large Loads that bring their own new capacity and have completed network upgrades; interim 
transmission service (i.e.,, non-firm transmission service for Large Loads that are in the process of 
meeting the requirements for firm service), and non-firm transmission service for flexible Large Loads 
that are willing and able to limit their use of the transmission system under certain conditions.   
 
In building the framework for these new transmission services, ISO-NE was able to capitalize 
on its DARD model,28 which will be used to register Large Loads.  This model allows the use of current 
ISO forecasting, telemetry, and dispatch tools, requiring minimal adaptation and resulting in expedited 
application.  Flexibility for non-firm transmission services will be achieved through a price-based 
re-dispatch mechanism.  Specifically, all or a portion of a Large Load’s non-firm transmission

d. Generation Studies 
To address this category of reform, the Tariff Revisions include a definition of Electrically 
Proximate Large Load, which is appropriately tailored to New England’s tightly networked 
transmission system (i.e., an injection into the New England transmission system from a Large 
Load Electrically Proximate Generator that is one or more substations away from a corresponding 
Electrically Proximate Large Load would likely not fully flow to the Electrically Proximate Large 
Load in a manner that is effectively as if the Electrically Proximate Large Load and Large Load 
Electrically Proximate Generator were located at the same point, or connected radially).  
Additionally, the ISO and the PTOs have developed rules for the interconnection of Large Load 
Co-Located Generators and Large Load Electrically Proximate Generators.  As explained in 
Section IV.C of this transmittal letter, the interconnection studies for these generators may be 
conducted concurrently with a Large Load System Impact Study.   
e. Cost Transparency 
To address this category of reform, the Tariff Revisions require the ISO to provide, develop, 
maintain, and post on its website, in an easily accessible, searchable and fillable format: (1) a 
cumulative list reflecting the Large Load Network Upgrades identified for each Large Load, 
categorized by upgrade type; and (2) costs estimates for each identified Large Load Network 
Upgrade for each Large Load.  In addition, as described in Section IV.D.2 of this transmittal letter,

b. 
Cost Allocation Mechanisms of the LLCRA 
 
The LLCRA utilizes four mechanisms to ensure that the costs of serving the Large Load Facility 
are not passed on to other transmission customers: (1) direct assignment of costs, both initial and 
ongoing, for the Direct Assignment Facilities; (2) payment of the Cost Recovery Charge when necessary 
to eliminate any transmission rate increases caused by the interconnection of the Large Load Facility 
and the construction of LLITO’s Network Upgrades; (3) payment of an Exit Fee, as applicable, upon 
termination of the LLCRA; and (4) adequate Credit Support to cover the cost of the Direct Assignment 
Facilities and LLITO’s Network Upgrades prior to commercial operation and the Exit Fee and all 
associated charges following commercial operation.  If the Large Load Eligible Customer and the Large 
Load Entity are the same entity, that entity is responsible under the LLCRA for these payments and the 
Credit Support. 
 
i. 
Direct Assignment Facilities 
 
The Direct Assignment Facilities, analogous to Interconnecting Transmission Owner’s 
Interconnection Facilities in a generator context, are sole-use facilities which will be constructed by the 
LLITO and paid for on a reimbursable basis by the Large Load Entity, consistent with the Commission’s 
cost-causation principles for sole-use facilities.  Following the construction of the Direct Assignment 
Facilities, the Large Load Entity will also pay for operation, maintenance, repair, and replacement of 
such facilities consistent with the individual LLITO’s methodology currently in place for analogous 
generator interconnection facilities.110

ii. 
Cost Recovery Charge 
 
The Cost Recovery Charge is the primary mechanism under which the PTOs will prevent cost 
shifts to other transmission customers caused by the interconnection of the Large Load Facility.  Under 
Article 10 and Appendix C-2 of the LLCRA, the Cost Recovery Charge will be billed monthly to the 
Large Load Entity and will be calculated in the following manner: 
Annual Cost Recovery Charge = Large Load Revenue Requirement – Applicable 
Transmission Service Payments 
The Large Load Revenue Requirement is the gross cost of LLITO’s Network Upgrades multiplied by 
the applicable Regional or Local Carrying Charge Factor and represents the revenue requirement impact 
of those upgrades.  The applicable transmission service payments are the payments made by the Large 
Load Eligible Customer for the applicable transmission service reserved on behalf of the Large Load 
Facility (FCDS, NFCDS, or ICDS).  This difference is the net impact of the upgrades on transmission 
rates, and payment (and associated crediting) of this amount holds other transmission customers 
harmless from the rate impacts of LLITO’s Network Upgrades. 
 
iii. 
Exit Fee 
 
In the event the LLCRA terminates and uncovered rate impacts remain for LLITO’s Network 
Upgrades, the Large Load Entity will pay the Exit Fee described in Article 10 and Appendix C-2.  The 
Exit Fee is equal to the Net Book Value of LLITO’s Network Upgrades along with Decommissioning 
Costs, and will, like the Cost Recovery Charge, be credited against the applicable transmission revenue 
requirement to avoid cost shifting to transmission customers. 
 
iv. 
Credit Support 
 
The LLCRA also requires the Large Load Entity to post sufficient financial assurance (“Credit 
Support”) both prior to commercial operation to cover the costs of the Direct Assignment Facilities and 
LLITO’s Network Upgrades111 as well as subsequent to commercial operation to cover the cost of the 
Exit Fee and any ongoing amounts due under the LLCRA.112  Due to differing financial assurance 
policies among the PTOs, the specific form, process, and amounts for Credit Support will be described 
in a PTO-specific Appendix D to be negotiated by the Parties, but nevertheless complying with Article 
10 of the LLCRA.  Provision of Credit Support throughout the term of the LLCRA will ensure that the 
LLITO is fully covered in the event of default or insolvency by the Large Load Entity, and in turn 
ensures that no costs caused by such default or insolvency will be passed on to other customers.

An interconnection customer's generating facility serving an Electrically Proximate Large 
Load or Co-Located Large Load in ISO-NE will be defined as a Large Load Co-Located Generator 
or Large Load Electrically Proximate Generator.  To align with the Show Cause Order’s 
considerations on cost shifting, the ISO proposes to meter Large Loads and any associated Large 
Load Co-Located Generator or Large Load Electrically Proximate Generator separately based on 
gross demand and gross supply, such that the two are not netted.  Large Load Co-Located 
Generators and Large Load Electrically Proximate Generators will be eligible to participate in the 
energy market, with some restrictions depending on how they are studied and their zero MW NRIS.  
 
As explained in Section IV.C of this transmittal letter, a Large Load Co-Located Generator 
or Large Load Electrically Proximate Generator has access to a new interconnection process that 
provides zero MWs of NRIS.  Under this process, the Large Load Co-Located Generator or Large 
Load Electrically Proximate Generator can be included in the same expedited 90-day study process 
as its associated Large Load.  This service allows the Large Load Co-Located Generator or Large 
Load Electrically Proximate Generator to achieve all or a portion of re-dispatch instructions for a 
Large Load receiving Non-Firm Contract Demand Service or Interim Contract Demand Service 
by injecting energy supply, consistent with the Non-Firm Large Load Generator Arrangement.  
However, this service does not allow the Large Load Co-Located Generators and Large Load 
Electrically Proximate Generator to net inject to the grid, because their net injections have not been 
studied.  Therefore, a Large Load Co-Located Generator or Large Load Electrically Proximate 
Generator may provide and receive credit for energy supply, on a gross supply basis, up to but not 
exceeding their associated Large Load’s gross demand. 
 
A Large Load Co-Located Generator and Large Load Electrically Proximate Generator 
may subsequently elect to participate in a Cluster Study in order to increase its Interconnection 
Service.  Through this process, the Large Load Co-Located Generator’s or Large Load Electrically 
Proximate Generator’s net injections are studied, which could result in NRIS greater than zero 
MWs.  Therefore, a Large Load Co-Located Generator or Large Load Electrically Proximate 
Generator that is subsequently studied in the cluster study process may provide and receive credit 
for energy supply, on a gross supply basis, in excess of their associated Large Load’s gross 
demand, but not exceeding their NRIS.   
 
The market mitigation rules in Market Rule 1 Appendix A, which apply to all other 
wholesale energy supply resources in ISO-NE, will apply to a Large Load Co-Located Generator 
and Large Load Electrically Proximate Generator.  These rules allow for consultation with the 
market monitor on resource-specific physical and financial parameters.  Large Load Co-Located 
Generators and Large Load Electrically Proximate Generators will be eligible to participate in the 
ancillary services markets, subject to the same requirements for other generators, including but not 
limited to capability auditing.

generating facilities are defined as Large Load Co-Located Generators and Large Load Electrically

interconnection pathway and an associated limited interconnection service that only provides zero 
MWs of NRIS.  This process allows ISO-NE to study a Co-Located Large Load or Electrically 
Proximate Large Load together with its associated Large Load Co-Located Generators or Large 
Load Electrically Proximate Generators in the same study, outside of the generation cluster study 
process.  Generating facilities that utilize this expedited interconnection pathway will be allowed 
to operate in parallel to the ISO-NE transmission system, but not be allowed to inject power to the 
grid, nor will they be given Capacity Network Resource Interconnection Service (“CNRIS”).  In
